newsitem.title: LEBANON: GDR surge raises Solidere share hopes.
newsitem.headline: GDR surge raises Solidere share hopes.

text.p: Daily demand for Solidere A shares has doubled on the Beirut Stock Exchange this week and sources close to the company said the surge was driven by a jump in the price of its Global Depositary Receipts in London.
The London price rise was driven in turn by demand for the GDRs from U.S. and European emerging market funds, the sources said.

They said the London price rise should have a knock-on effect on the price of the shares in Beirut which have languished for two years after their spectacular debut in 1994 and are widely considered to be heavily undervalued.
Solidere, which is rebuilding central Beirut, is Lebanon's biggest company and accounts for $2.2 billion of the total $2.4 billion capitalisation of the Beirut Stock Exchange.
However, some Beirut brokers said the GDRs' performance was unlikely to affect the shares in Beirut, which they did not expect to move significantly for several more months.

Daily turnover in the A shares, issued to former owners of property rights in central Beirut which Solidere is rebuilding, has ranged this week between 88,000 and 109,000 shares from 40-50,000 a day in recent weeks.
Despite this, the A shares remained on Wednesday at their all-time low of $10.25 while B shares, issued in a $650 million flotation in 1994, were also low at $10.75.
In London, the GDRs reached $12.8 on Wednesday after rising since Friday from $11.05, the low to which they dropped from their issue price of $11.50 last November.
"If there is big demand for the GDRs in London at $2.50 above the share price in Beirut, that should be expected to have a knock-on effect on the shares," the source close to Solidere told Reuters.

He declined to comment on the increased Beirut demand for A shares, the cheaper of the two shares. However, a market source said: "Presumably people are buying now because there is a lot of supply at a very cheap price and there is movement in London."

But a broker with a Beirut bank doubted that the Solidere shares would follow the GDRs upwards in the short term although a Merrill Lynch research in January said they were undervalued by 43 percent and recommended them as a long term buy.

"Definitely the Solidere GDR in London is finding some interest, because there is interest in Lebanon and any fund manager who wants to invest here needs a highly capitalised stock to invest in, and Solidere is the only one," the broker said.
"But as foreigners they cannot buy Solidere shares and they also prefer to buy on their own market rather than Beirut," he said.
"We need time for Solidere shares to rise because they haven't finished distributing the A shares and there is no peace agreement in the Middle East", the broker added.
"I don't see any favourable price move in Beirut for six months."
The source close to Solidere said it had issued 85 percent of the 117 million A shares, whose distribution has flooded the market since 1994 and helped depress the prices of both shares.
"I think the distribution will be complete in the first half of the year," the source said.
